title: Galaxy Cluster IRC 0218 (clean)
caption: Galaxy cluster IRC 0218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, K.-V. Tran (Texas A&M University), and K. Wong (Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy & Astrophysics)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble image shows IRC 0218, a distant cluster of galaxies in the constellation Eridanus. One of its brightest members is a monster elliptical galaxy, seen as it looked 9.6 billion years ago, that acts as a natural magnifying glass. When it was found, it was the most distant lensing galaxy known, beating the previous record holder by 200 million years.

Its gravity bends, magnifies and distorts light from a tiny spiral galaxy behind it, which is going through a rapid burst of star formation. Light from that background galaxy took 10.7 billion years to reach us. Hubble pictures in blue wavelengths showed a blue, eyebrow-shaped object beside a smeared blue dot around the big elliptical, the stretched images of the farther galaxy.

By gauging how strongly the lens bends light, astronomers weighed the elliptical at 180 billion times the Sun's mass, a heavyweight for its era. Surprisingly, it holds little dark matter compared with closer elliptical galaxies. The team suspects it will keep growing over the next 9 billion years by swallowing neighbouring galaxies.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFC3 cameras. NASA shows F475W in blue, F814W in green, and F105W, F125W and F160W in red.
understand.eye: The image combines 3.3 hours of exposure and includes near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

explore: Kim-Vy Tran of Texas A&M University spotted the lens while studying star formation in distant clusters. Spectra from the W.M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii showed hot hydrogen gas, a sign of star birth, apparently coming from an old galaxy that had stopped forming stars long ago. The young stars turned out to lie much farther away, behind the elliptical.
